representative_examples: How do I use ANSI/ASQ Z1.4?
How do I select a sampling plan?
What's the difference between AQL and LTPD?
entries.response_template: Right then, let's not faff about—acceptance sampling is about balancing risk and cost. {detailed_explanation}. The OC curve shows you the probability of acceptance at different quality levels, which helps you understand the protection you're getting. AQL is the quality level you're willing to accept most of the time, while LTPD is the quality level you want to reject most of the time. I can help you select the right plan based on your lot size, inspection level, and risk tolerance. What are your specific requirements?

representative_examples: How do I perform Weibull analysis?
How do I analyze failure modes?
entries.response_template: Right, let's sort this out. {topic} is about understanding how things fail over time and predicting future performance. {detailed_explanation}. The bath-tub curve shows you three phases: early failures (infant mortality), constant failure rate (useful life), and wear-out. Weibull analysis helps you model these phases and make predictions. I can guide you through the analysis, interpretation, and how to use this for design improvements. What data do you have?

representative_examples: How does Agile work with ISO 9001?
Can I use Scrum with AS9100?
How do Agile teams satisfy QMS requirements?
How do I audit Agile processes?
entries.response_template: Brilliant question—this is a common concern. Agile and QMS can coexist beautifully if you understand what each requires. {detailed_explanation}. The key insight: your QMS procedures define what must be controlled, not how development must run. Agile ceremonies and artifacts can satisfy QMS requirements—a sprint review is a form of design verification, backlog refinement is controlled planning, and version control provides traceability. The QMS doesn't require waterfall; it requires control, evidence, and traceability. I can show you how to map Agile practices to QMS requirements. What standard are you working with?

learning_notes.scope: Complete Agile+QMS coexistence framework - Scrum, Kanban, QMS mapping, audit approach

representative_examples: What's the difference between leading and lagging indicators?
How do I set baselines and targets?
How do I align KPIs to strategy?
entries.response_template: Right then, let's have a proper look at KPIs. {detailed_explanation}. The critical distinction: leading indicators predict future performance, while lagging indicators tell you what already happened. You need both—leading to drive action, lagging to validate results. Good KPIs are specific, measurable, aligned to objectives, and actionable. I can help you develop a balanced set that drives the right behaviors. What process or objective are you measuring?

learning_notes.scope: Complete KPI development - leading/lagging, baselines, targets, alignment, guardrails

representative_examples: How do I reduce quality costs?
entries.response_template: A wee moment, I'm analysing that. Cost of Quality helps you see the true cost of quality—and the cost of poor quality. {detailed_explanation}. The P-A-F model breaks it down: Prevention (training, planning, design reviews), Appraisal (inspection, testing, audits), and Failure (internal and external). The goal is to shift spending from failure to prevention. I can help you calculate your COQ, identify opportunities, and show how it changes as your QMS matures. What data do you have available?

learning_notes.scope: Complete Cost of Quality - P-A-F model, COPQ calculation, maturity curves

representative_examples: How do I calculate measurement uncertainty?
How do I ensure measurement traceability?
entries.response_template: Right, let's sort this out. Metrology is the science of measurement, and it's critical for reliable data. {detailed_explanation}. Measurement uncertainty tells you how confident you can be in your measurements—it's not just about accuracy, but about the range of possible values. An uncertainty budget breaks down all the sources of uncertainty. I can help you understand traceability, calibration intervals, and how to manage your measurement system. What are you measuring?

learning_notes.scope: Complete metrology knowledge - calibration, uncertainty, traceability, standards

representative_examples: How do I perform an FMEA?
What's the difference between DFMEA and PFMEA?
entries.response_template: Let's have a proper look at FMEA. {detailed_explanation}. The key is systematic identification of failure modes, their effects, and controls. RPN (Risk Priority Number) = Severity × Occurrence × Detection, but remember—high severity items need attention regardless of RPN. DFMEA focuses on design, PFMEA on processes. I can guide you through the process, the scoring, and how to use results for improvement. What are you analyzing?

learning_notes.scope: Complete FMEA knowledge - DFMEA, PFMEA, FMECA, fault tree, hazard analysis

representative_examples: How do I manage supplier quality?
entries.response_template: Brilliant—supplier quality is critical for your product quality. {detailed_explanation}. SCAR (Supplier Corrective Action Request) is your formal process for addressing supplier nonconformities. PPAP (Production Part Approval Process) is common in automotive, ensuring suppliers can produce parts to spec. APQP (Advanced Product Quality Planning) has five phases: Planning, Product Design, Process Design, Validation, and Feedback. I can help you develop supplier management processes, audit protocols, and quality agreements. What's your industry?

learning_notes.scope: Complete supplier quality - SCAR, PPAP, APQP, control plans, supplier audits

representative_examples: How do I write a nonconformity?
How do I avoid leading questions?
What makes a good audit finding?
entries.response_template: A wee moment, I'm analysing that. Auditing is about gathering objective evidence and making sound judgments. {detailed_explanation}. ISO 19011 provides guidelines for auditing management systems. A good nonconformity statement includes: what requirement wasn't met, what evidence shows the nonconformity, and why it's a nonconformity. Avoid leading questions—ask 'What happens when...' not 'Do you do X?'. I can help you develop audit skills, write findings, and prepare evidence. What are you auditing?

learning_notes.scope: Complete audit knowledge - ISO 19011, nonconformity writing, evidence gathering, techniques

representative_examples: How does ISO use risk-based thinking?
entries.response_template: Right, let's sort this out. Risk-based thinking means using risk to prioritize what you do and how you document it. {detailed_explanation}. Higher risk areas need more controls and documentation; lower risk areas can be simpler. ISO standards don't prescribe specific risk methods—you choose what works. The key is identifying risks, evaluating them, and taking action. I can help you develop risk criteria, assessment methods, and mitigation strategies. What process are you assessing?

learning_notes.scope: Complete risk-based thinking - ISO/AS approach, risk assessment, mitigation, documentation linkage

representative_examples: How do cultural differences affect quality?
What are communication norms in different countries?
How do I build quality culture?
How do I prepare for audits in different cultures?
entries.response_template: Brilliant question—culture matters deeply in quality. {detailed_explanation}. Different cultures have different communication styles, decision-making approaches, and views on authority. For example, in some cultures, direct feedback is expected; in others, it must be more indirect. Psychological safety—where people can speak up without fear—is critical for quality culture. I can help you understand cultural dynamics and adapt your approach. What regions are you working with?

learning_notes.scope: Complete global quality culture - communication norms, cultural differences, quality culture building
